utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Madam Vidovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, again, the witness stated clearly yesterday and repeated today that he and the Command received information from the assistant for security, and that is not in any contradiction with this, and I'm still claiming that the witness is being confused.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... the question is allowed and the objection is overruled. Carry on, Mr. Neuner.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Could you tell me, since you said in the Hadzihasanovic trial: "I did not follow the course of the investigation because I was prevented from doing that by the combat activities," how could you have yesterday remembered all the individual steps by the Military Security Service?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Objection, Your Honour. The witness never said that he remembered all the steps taken by the Security Service. He spoke of Asim Delalic's report, that is, he was the assistant commander for morale, so I'm objecting again.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: I just want to put another portion to you. First of all, I didn't hear that you looked at Asim Delalic's report.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Did you say so, as suggested by my learned colleague?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I just said I think the witness can answer that question, if you talk about somebody.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Did you -- it was suggested here. Did you have occasion to look at a report from Mr. Delalic, as suggested by my learned colleague?

utterances.speaker: HALIM HUSIC
utterances.text: No. I will repeat, and this is not the first time, the commander had ordered an investigation and the assistant commander informed the Corps Command at a meeting about the details of this investigation, about what he had done so far and what he was able to establish.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: But why didn't you say all these steps you were listing yesterday, why didn't you say that in the Hadzihasanovic case, if this had indeed been the case that at the meeting in Krpeljici, Mr. Delalic had reported about everything already?

utterances.speaker: HALIM HUSIC
utterances.text: Because I did not take part in them.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: But that's exactly my point --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Madam Vidovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Objection, Your Honour. Persistently, the Prosecutor is trying to suggest to this witness that he was -- that he stated that he discussed different measures that had been undertaken, and the witness only spoke about the same thing that he has mentioned today, about the report submitted by Asim Delalic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Sorry. I thought -- Ms. Vidovic, I thought I had clarified this with the witness, that he did not see any report from Mr. Asim Delalic, is that right, because you're coming again by stating that he had seen this report.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Is it correct, did you see or did you not see a report? I'm clarifying your point, Mrs. Vidovic, because you just brought it up. I'm sorry, I'm trying to find a way out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, ma'am.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the Prosecutor is now trying to confuse me. A report may be -- and I'm using the term "report" which has the same meaning anywhere in the world, including in Germany, a report can be either written or oral. Nowhere was there any mention of a written report. It was an oral report, and he's really trying to confuse me now. This is not fair, and we're wasting a lot of time and we're never going to finish with this witness. He will have to stay over the weekend because of these interventions by my colleague.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: If he has to stay over the weekend, so be it, but we need to get to the bottom of this. Mr. Neuner, you are said to be confusing the counsel and confusing the witness. Do you have any response to that?

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Now that my colleague has mentioned an oral report, I will try to put this on board. I believe before it was mentioned before that this was an oral report. But the issue of the Prosecution is that the steps which have been reported yesterday, in the witness's testimony, had not been reported -- or had not been testified about at the time when this witness testified in the Hadzihasanovic case, and I think I can almost leave it here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: In fact, I was going to say, if you stayed on what the witness said yesterday, I know you've mentioned it a little earlier when you detailed him -- told him the details of what actions were taken. If you stayed on that and kept on reminding Madam Vidovic, we probably would not be having this problem, and remind Madam Vidovic that that's what you're talking about. You're talking about the testimony yesterday and how it differs from the testimony in the Hadzihasanovic case. You're not talking about any reports.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Correct. I was just trying to take the suggestion from my learned colleague on board, but I will move on. I'm practically done. I just want to read a last passage from the Hadzihasanovic case, and it's on the same page, to this witness. And this is line 18. And there, in your answer, you said: "Now, who it was, with whom and to what extent conducted that investigation, I am not able to tell you because I wasn't there."

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Is it not correct that you were not in a position --

utterances.speaker: HALIM HUSIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Sorry --

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, could my learned Colleague Neuner please -- and let me say, first of all, whenever I present portions of a transcript to a witness who does not speak English, we would have a translation ready so that the witness can be acquainted with the context. In this situation, the Prosecutor Neuner is just cherry-picking, he's cherry-picked one sentence here, and I would urge him to read the entire response that the witness gave and not just pick and choose individual sentences out of context. And in the future, Your Honour, if I may suggest that we should have a translation into Bosnian as well so that the witness can understand what it is all about. And I think this has been the practice so far in this Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: If I may respond, the court session yesterday was going on until 7.00, and the part of his testimony which I am trying to dwell on was, so to speak, ready for my notice only after 7.00, and I had no translation service on such a short notice available overnight until this morning, 9.00, to translate the English portions of the transcript in the Hadzihasanovic case into the Bosnian version. We would certainly have endeavoured to do that, but I, myself, needed to identify them first, because I, myself, was also confronted with this evidence from yesterday, only since a few hours. If this is at all possible, we would have done it, but as I said, the circumstances didn't allow for that. I will take my learned colleague's suggestion on board and will just read out the question as well as the entire answer now and ask the witness to comment upon it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Please do, Mr. Neuner.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: But before you do so, Mr. Neuner, I need to understand whether this entire discussion goes to the credibility of the witness or whether it goes to the substance of the matter; namely, the question of whether or not an investigation was actually made into the massacre at Bikosi, and whether the witness knew about this investigation and the result of it. So what are we considering here?

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: It certainly goes to the substance of the issue, whether there was an investigation and what steps in the course of that investigation were undertaken, as well as to a certain degree Your Honours have followed the course of cross-examination, also to the credibility of this witness. So in that light, I will read out the question, the entire question, and the answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Just before you read it, just give us the reference of the question again on this transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: It is transcript page 10935, lines 11 and following until 19: "We had a witness before you came, Mr. Siljak, who was also of the 306th Brigade," Judge Swart asks, "and he says the investigation into the events on -- that may have occurred in Maline was done by Mr. Delalic. Is that right?" The answer then is: "He was assistant commander for security, and it was his obligation to do that. He reported to the commander on the events that had to do with the overall security and disruptions that may have impaired the security. Now, who it was, with whom and to what extent conducted that investigation, I am not able to tell you because I wasn't there."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is what I still maintain, and we were informed about this investigation by Mr. Delalic at the Command. And as for the investigation itself, who conducted it, how, and in what manner, I have to repeat, I don't know, I wasn't there, I was busy with other things.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: But the Prosecution's point is yesterday you stated something else. On page 39, and I'm just reading the portion to you: "We really wanted to establish this, and both the police and the Security Service, but also other services of the brigade, because this was addressed to us, this was at our expense because it had happened in our area of responsibility, all these services really wanted to establish the truth. I know this, because we sent policemen who had been intercepted, we sent them to try and identify, among these -- from among these armed groups, to identify the people by observing those areas, where they moved, through which they are moved. However, we were never able to find out the exact information." Aren't you describing the course of the investigation here?

utterances.speaker: HALIM HUSIC
utterances.text: Yes, in the manner that we -- as we were informed by the assistant commander for security. And when I say "we," "us," I mean all of us in the Brigade Command, because we were a team that had a task to carry out, and part of that task was something that the Command had to carry out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Neuner, I think it is pointless to go on about this aspect. The Chamber has now got all it needs in order to assess the situation itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Yes. I was about to say the Prosecution has no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Neuner. Any re-examination, Madam Vidovic?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just briefly, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, let us just dwell on this last issue of investigation into Maline. Tell us, please, is it correct that what you were describing here, you were describing what you had heard from Mr. Delalic?

utterances.speaker: HALIM HUSIC
utterances.text: Yes, the way he had informed the Command and the commander, that is what I mentioned yesterday and that's what I talked about.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: The next question: Did you, at any point during your testimony yesterday and today, mention or not that you knew which military policemen or who exactly did what during this investigation?

utterances.speaker: HALIM HUSIC
utterances.text: No, absolutely not, never, because everywhere in the world the security services conducting an investigation will not provide any information to anyone who is not directly involved.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please, do you see any difference between what you have said here and what you said in Hadzihasanovic before, any difference in those reports or testimonies?

utterances.speaker: HALIM HUSIC
utterances.text: No, absolutely none.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: And now just briefly, Mr. Husic, I would like to go back to the statement that was shown to you on a number of times today, PT6254. Mr. Husic, could you please do the following: First, items 8 and 9, page 06323793, that will be on the third page of this statement in the Bosnian version, but also on the English version, Mr. Husic, would you please describe to the honourable Judges how this interview with the Prosecution evolved, how many times were you -- for how many days were you questioned, and how many times did you have to interfere with corrections?

utterances.speaker: HALIM HUSIC
utterances.text: Yes. I was called by the Prosecutor in Sarajevo to report to their offices, and we agreed -- I think it was Tuesday, and I got there on the first day after having worked from 7.00 to 2.00 in the morning, and we remained there until 7.00 p.m. with me providing my statement. They promised that they would translate that portion for the next day. So then the next day, I had to work again between 7.00 and 2.00 a.m. I went to the offices again, spent some time there. I can't remember how many hours. I brought with me the portion of -- I took with me the first part of my statement so that I could enter any corrections, so that in these couple of days I actually worked for over 20 hours a day.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: I asked you whether this statement, the Bosnian version, was corrected once or on several -- at several levels, several times.

utterances.speaker: HALIM HUSIC
utterances.text: It had to be -- it was done once, but there were many corrections. There were a lot of corrections that had to be made. I did correct it once, but it was very difficult to do the corrections. There were many of them. That's the point.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: You said that your statement was incorrect. What do you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: HALIM HUSIC
utterances.text: What I mean by that is after my first statement, when I spoke in Bosnian and the Prosecutor received this in English, then somebody re-told the whole thing in Bosnian, and when I received that version in Bosnian, it was very difficult, especially because the questions were missing, it was very difficult to correct this statement the way I wanted to do it. It was a very tiring task. I could not formulate new sentences, but the answers that I gave, I wasn't really satisfied with the way they were written down.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: You did sign the statement. How many days did you spend with the Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: HALIM HUSIC
utterances.text: Three or 4 days. On the fourth day, I brought the corrections to my statement.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: So I conclude that you worked on this for four days, and here we see that there were 16 or 17 days of the statement. Whatever the case may have been, we saw item 8 of this statement. Could you please take a look at it? It was about the elements of the 1st and 4th Battalion of the 306th Brigade. Would you now please take a look at item 9. The Prosecutor confronted you with a portion, claiming that you said that elements of the 1st and 4th Battalion of the 306th Brigade, who were not engaged on the defence lines in Vlasici, together with civilians, began the lifting of blockade, and now I would like you to take a look at number 9. You said: "These were informal groups. I know that there was one group from Visnjevo, another one from Dub, another one from Suhi Dol. Part of them were members of the 306th Brigade from those villages. They were civilians." Please tell us, did you explain to the Prosecutor at that time the same things that you said here today?

utterances.speaker: HALIM HUSIC
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely, and I would like the Prosecutor to show his questions that he had put, where I gave this answer under item 8. This was a group -- it wasn't a portion of the brigade, part of the brigade. They were local civilians. Some of them were in the 306th Brigade. They weren't part of the brigade, but individuals who were at the same time members of the brigade, but on this occasion they came as village units, after these alarming events, to help and assist the population, the local villagers who had been under attack.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Vidovic. Judge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, you told us yesterday that some of the soldiers of the 306th Brigade abandoned the brigade in order to join the El Mudjahedin Detachment. Do you remember that? Do you remember saying that?

utterances.speaker: HALIM HUSIC
utterances.text: Yes, individuals did that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I wanted to know whether the Brigade Command did anything to try and react in the face of these --

utterances.speaker: HALIM HUSIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- brigade.

utterances.speaker: HALIM HUSIC
utterances.text: Yes, we did do something about it. Throughout this time, because of various circumstances, we had stockades full of soldiers or fighters who were not disciplined, who infracted [as interpreted] on the discipline. We had the case where the military police of the 306th Brigade, in the course of their duties, killed members of the 306th Brigade who did not abide by the regulations that were in force.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Was there any official, formal follow-up to these reactions? Were people punished, sanctioned, steps of which there would be official traces anywhere? I'm still speaking about these people leaving the brigade, only about that.

utterances.speaker: HALIM HUSIC
utterances.text: We considered those individuals deserters. The military police brought them in detention. Some of them were sanctioned, and they were kept in military detention. But I can't tell you the exact numbers, but there were criminal reports also raised against some of them. And you can check this in the documents of the brigade.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I apologise. The answer, as it appears in the transcript, does not reflect what the witness had said. He said that some of them were --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Just a second.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- punished, and disciplinary measures were taken, and here there's no mention of disciplinary mention.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Line 60 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Witness, would you repeat the answer. Apparently you have not been translated correctly. Could you just repeat the answer that you were giving?

utterances.speaker: HALIM HUSIC
utterances.text: Yes. All those individuals who deserted the unit we considered as deserters, and different measures were taken against them. Sometimes these measures were disciplinary measures, but there were even criminal reports submitted against some of them, although I couldn't tell you exactly what that number was at this point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Is that the correct answer now?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just one more small thing in this regard, sir. They were arrested -- like they went to the detachment to take those men out, to put them in detention, to punish them?

utterances.speaker: HALIM HUSIC
utterances.text: No, that would have been very dangerous. I tried to tell you yesterday that up until the autumn of 1993, we did not have uniforms. We could see -- you could see that in the video clip yesterday. On that day, when I spoke outside of that monastery, I came from the brigade. I was at work on that day, but I was dressed in civilian clothing, because we didn't have uniforms. After we've done something, we would go back to our homes. When we call someone up to report to the unit and he does not report, as soon as he would get back to his house, the military police would arrest him; and I mentioned that my colleague --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: We're five minutes away from the break. Shall we take our break now? We'll take a break and continue answering the question later when you come back. Court adjourned and come back in half.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Judge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sorry, I was trying to remember your answer, your last answer. So it was confirmed to me that you could not enter the Mujahedin camp in order to arrest those individuals. There were some who left the Mujahedin Detachment in order to join the brigade, after the sanctions -- those steps were taken, were they.

utterances.speaker: HALIM HUSIC
utterances.text: Probably, but I'm afraid I'm not able to list their names.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. One last question. With regard to the video clip we saw yesterday, we saw the Guca Gora monastery. You were referring to it in your answer today. Please remind me, was this footage filmed after the slight damage to the monastery, inside the monastery?

utterances.speaker: HALIM HUSIC
utterances.text: Yes. Actually, as soon as units of the BH Army entered Guca Gora, a number of people, immediately after that -- we entered in the morning, and then in the afternoon a number of men entered the monastery -- or, rather, the yard of the monastery, where there were several vehicles, and they entered to seize those vehicles. And someone used paint that was in the monastery, and the paint was spilled. We tried to clean it up, but we couldn't, because it was permanent paint. As for the equipment in the rooms and in the offices and the organ, there were minor damages.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, thank you for this information, but I wanted to know something else. Among the ABiH units, was there also the El Mudjahedin Detachment that took part in the takeover operation of Guca Gora?

utterances.speaker: HALIM HUSIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Were there individual Mujahedins who would have come from other units, who were at any rate fighting the enemy, the enemy of Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: HALIM HUSIC
utterances.text: No, not on those days when we were taking control of Guca Gora. But when defence lines were established below Guca Gora, a certain number of those persons, those foreigners, did enter Guca Gora. A group even settled there. And we discussed this, because the civilian authorities were in charge, but the military police guarded only the monastery. We couldn't guard the whole settlement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Husic, I would like to return to an issue that I have raised with you before; namely, the attempts made by the 3rd Corps to somehow put the foreigners -- the foreign fighters under some sort of control. The picture that we have been offered here during this trial is that Mujahedin soldiers entered into Bosnia and Herzegovina and formed small groups here and there, and took part in a more or less coordinated manner with the ABiH in the combat operations. We also heard that one of these groups was stationed in Mehurici and that they were established as a detachment within the 3rd Corps in August 1993, I think it was. But we have also heard that all along, from the very moment these fighters came into the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina, there were a variety of problems. Some of them had to do with the coordination and the cooperation with the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina. Other problems related to the contacts that these foreign groups had with the local population. Some other problems had to do with, shall I say, civilian crimes committed by these gentlemen, and some other problems again actually had to do with war crimes committed. So we understand that there was or there were all along a number of difficulties in fitting these foreign fighters into -- somehow into cooperation with the army. And my question to you is: What did the 3rd Corps do to bring the situation under the control from the moment they were present, let's say from the month of June 1993 and until the end of the war? Do you have some sort of idea of what was done at the corps level?

utterances.speaker: HALIM HUSIC
utterances.text: You saw, in the reports I sent as assistant commander from the 306th Mountain Brigade, that this was a problem that we repeatedly drew attention to. The Command of the 3rd Corps, regarding the decision to form the detachment, as it was explained to us, was made to put them under their control. However, even after the formation of the detachment, all the foreigners didn't join that detachment. They operated not only as humanitarian organisations outside the detachment, but occasionally certain armed groups would rally locals from various parts of Bosnia-Herzegovina and they would act as armed groups. Opposing those armed groups by units of the BH Army would produce tensions which could lead to conflicts between our units and the local population, and this simply could not be overcome. And we said what was the most important reason that the civilians were tied to these people was the humanitarian aid they provided. They had large funds. They supplied clothing and food. They often engaged in arms sales. So they made it possible for the people to get hold of weapons, and these were activities which it is very difficult to eliminate in a situation of war.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: So you're saying that despite the facts that also the local population felt occasionally intimidated by these gentlemen, despite these problems, the local population nevertheless accepted their presence in the territory because of the advantages that they could get from the foreign fighters; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: HALIM HUSIC
utterances.text: Yes. And as an illustration of this, allow me to tell you that, among other things, they offered people who joined in marriage on the basis of the Sharia law, they would give them 100 or 200 German Marks as a reward, so that people who may have been living fro 20 or 30 years married, they would again take their marriage vows under the Sharia. And there were many such examples whereby they linked the local populations to themselves, they attracted them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: I see. So from a military point of view, this must have been a nightmare, because if I were to lead, and I'm not a military leader I might confess right away, but if I were to lead a military operation, and then suddenly in the middle of the whole operation an uncontrolled armed group shows up on the battle scene and interferes in the battle, that might cause confusion and, in fact, danger, and that is -- that would be something that any military commander would seek to avoid, if possible. So how did the 306th Brigade, to start there, how did your brigade seek to deal with this?

utterances.speaker: HALIM HUSIC
utterances.text: I have to say, first of all, that the proportion of highly-educated inhabitants in the Bila Valley was not more than 5 per cent. In the total population, we had five men with certain military know how, the brigade commander who was a lieutenant, the assistant for educational matters, who was a captain, and three guys who, as battalion commanders, were students of military academies, but they interrupted their studies because of the war. All the others in the brigade were civilians. The population of which the brigade consisted had about 50 per cent of people with a secondary education, and the rest only had elementary education. Until the autumn of 1993, we wore civilian clothing and weapons that we had purchased ourselves. A very small percentage, maybe some 50 rifles, came from the Municipality Territorial Defence Staff. And in view of such a situation, with three or four times more inhabitants in the valley than the regular population, it was a real nightmare. But in view of matters such as food, clothing, weapons, and all these other links that these foreigners had established with the local people, neither we nor the civilian authorities that we brought pressure to bear on could not resolve the situation, because this was the only helping hand that was extended to us as a people in those parts and at that time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: My question to you was: What did the 306th Brigade Command do in order to reduce danger during the combat operations, danger arising out of the fact that intervention by foreign and unorganised groups might be present at the battle scene?

utterances.speaker: HALIM HUSIC
utterances.text: We didn't have much opportunity. There was not much we could do, and there was not much that we did. We tried, wherever and whenever possible, through the civilian authorities and in other ways to influence them to correct their behaviour. My section, whose task it was to act politically in the unit and to enter into contact with the political authorities in the social community, did that. But in concrete military terms, to oppose their activities that were at our expense, we didn't have much of a chance to do anything.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Tell us more about the meetings you had with -- in the civil sphere in order to try and get a better grasp and control over the situation. What did you actually do?

utterances.speaker: HALIM HUSIC
utterances.text: A large number of such meetings were held. First of all, we would meet with the Croatian population to try and suppress the propaganda about the Mujahedin and to try and persuade them that they weren't such a threat as the media portrayed it. Secondly, we insisted --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Can I interrupt you there. Did the media portray the Mujahedin fighters as a threat in autumn 1993?

utterances.speaker: HALIM HUSIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. The media, especially the Croatian media, very early on started talking about the enormous danger as of the new year, that is, the beginning of 1993, and they were saying that the Croatian population of the Bila Valley were threatened by the Mujahedin. In those days, they were not such a major factor, and we persuaded them that units of the BH Army would protect the entire population of the Bila Valley. However, the propaganda intensified with time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: You were telling us about the meetings, and I interrupted you, so, please, I would like you to explain to us again the steps that were taken by the 306th Brigade by calling meetings with the civilian and local authorities and representatives of the Mujahedin, I imagine, in order to control -- tell us more about what exactly was done and how it resulted.

utterances.speaker: HALIM HUSIC
utterances.text: Not much was done. We were repeatedly given promises that they -- or, rather, the part that collaborated with the civilian authorities would prevent such incidents. And then, when another incident occurred, they would disassociate themselves from such an incident so that we didn't have any control over those activities. I do know that when they were in the school and when they complained about our battalion and they wanted our battalion to be removed from the school, and the 306th Brigade refused to do that, they resolutely protested with the civilian authorities, and they abandoned the school. So occasionally they, in collaboration with the civilian authorities, they would bring pressure to bear on us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Who gave you the assurances?

utterances.speaker: HALIM HUSIC
utterances.text: I don't quite understand which assurances you're referring to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I was unclear. You told us just a while ago that from time to time, you would get assurances from either the civilian authorities or from the Mujahedin that future incidents would not occur, and I'm just curious to know which -- who gave you those assurances. Would that be local clerics or the Mujahedin themselves?

utterances.speaker: HALIM HUSIC
utterances.text: The civilian authorities. We required the civilian authorities to take steps, and their response was that without the material aid arriving through the mediation of the Mujahedin, they couldn't survive, but that the Mujahedin had promised them that they would put an end to certain activities which we considered to be bad.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Did anyone from the 306th Command ever sit down in a meeting with Mujahedin representatives present?

utterances.speaker: HALIM HUSIC
utterances.text: I'm not quite sure about that, but possibly, in the period when the El Mujahid Detachment was about to be formed, when these discussions were conducted with them, that someone from the 306th Mountain Brigade may have taken part in those discussions, but I'm not sure. I didn't. If someone did, then it would have been the commander. But they didn't like the commander or any member of the 306th Brigade, because they saw us as a threat to their activities. They had a hostile attitude towards us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm sorry I'm pulling this out, but it's important for us to understand just how it worked out in practice. Let me get back to the issue of your reports to the 3rd Corps Command. You said that you frequently brought the problems to the attention of the 3rd Corps; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: HALIM HUSIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: At a later stage, and I know that at a much later stage you, yourself, joined the 3rd Corps, so were you aware of how the 3rd Corps dealt with the information that they got? And I would appreciate if you could divide your answer as to what did the 3rd Corps do with the information they got from you -- from the 306th Brigade before you, yourself, were employed with the 3rd Corps, and then after you, yourself, were positioned at the 3rd Corps Command.

utterances.speaker: HALIM HUSIC
utterances.text: Yes. Well, regarding bodies for morale in the 3rd Corps would receive reports from all the units, including the 306th, and then on the basis of all those reports, they would prepare a summary with the key issues, the issues that they considered to be important would be put in a new report which would then be forwarded to a higher-level command. And at meetings between the Corps Command, the assistant commander for morale would inform the commander and the rest of the Command about factors affecting combat morale, and those reports would include what he considered to be a priority or important from the reports supplied by the subordinate units.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: But do you know whether, in fact, the information or some of the information that was passed up to the 3rd Corps from the 306th Brigade, was that -- information relating to the Mujahedin, was that ever passed on to the superior level of command, which would have been the Supreme Commander, I would imagine? Do you know if any of the information that came from you was ever passed on to the top?

utterances.speaker: HALIM HUSIC
utterances.text: No, I really don't know that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: You don't know that for the time you were with the 306th Brigade?

utterances.speaker: HALIM HUSIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, when you said I forwarded reports to the Command.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: But what was the situation when you, yourself, were at the 3rd Corps level? Did you then pass on information about the activities and level of cooperation with the Mujahedin to the Supreme Command?

utterances.speaker: HALIM HUSIC
utterances.text: Yes. The Department for Morale of the Supreme Command was informed about this lack of cooperation by the El Mudjahedin Detachment. However, this was not a problem that anyone seriously addressed at the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Why not?

utterances.speaker: HALIM HUSIC
utterances.text: I cannot know that. The assistant commanders in the Supreme Command Staff may know that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: But can I ask you, I mean, was the -- the relations with the Mujahedin, not only the Mujahedin Detachment but also the other Mujahedin groups, was that something that people were talking about at the 306th Brigade level and at the 3rd Corps level on a daily basis, I mean, or did it never come up?

utterances.speaker: HALIM HUSIC
utterances.text: Yes, it was regularly discussed as a problem, but this was a situation in which, on the one hand, you have all the things coming through humanitarian organisations, and they were numerous, and it was a precondition for our survival, and on the other hand, you have the problems provoked by them. And in view of such a balance of forces, the population was divided, too. The civilian authorities, and especially the MUP, the police, were not satisfied with their activities. They could not control them, and a major problem was that we knew that among them there were a certain number of men who contacted centres outside Bosnia-Herzegovina, Milan, Vienna, Zagreb, and the Military Security Services did inform corps commands of this. But, on the other hand, everything else that came through humanitarian aid, and as a result of their cooperation with the population, was at the other end. So a decision had to be made, which was really a difficult decision to make. And when yesterday we spoke about the disbanding of the detachment, we saw with what attention and what a vast quantity of problems existed, because a fresh conflict was threatening in Central Bosnia on the eve of the Dayton Accords themselves.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: What are you referring to? "A fresh conflict was threatening in Central Bosnia." Which conflict?

utterances.speaker: HALIM HUSIC
utterances.text: When the 3rd Corps commander began to suggest to representatives of the El Mujahid Detachment that the detachment needed to be disbanded, they forcefully rejected this. He was informed about the permanent session of the shura within the detachment, and this is a body that actually commanded the unit, and they were receiving orders from the centres in Milan or -- they were in contact with many centres. I cannot know individually which one of them had the most influence on this group.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: My last question is: Did the perception of the military cooperation with the -- between the 3rd Corps and the El Mujahid Detachment change over the years from 1993 to 1995?

utterances.speaker: HALIM HUSIC
utterances.text: We were hoping that with the forming of a unit, all the armed foreigners would in that way be under control. This didn't happen, however. Certain individual armed groups remained outside the El Mujahid Detachment and continued to create numerous problems. On the other hand, no matter how much we tried to place the El Mujahid Detachment in the system of control and -- command and control, this did not happen until the end of the war, until the detachment was actually disbanded. Our hopes were really illusory.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: So I understand, just to clarify your last answer, that the level of cooperation in military operations was the same from the time when the detachment was established until the end of the war. I mean, my question is: Did it, over time, become easier to cooperate with them, or were they still, as you say, uncontrollable?

utterances.speaker: HALIM HUSIC
utterances.text: Officially, they were impossible to control. The only way in which a certain number of people were able to have some cooperation or influence was if they personally respected him, if they personally gained trust and got to know that person. Otherwise, no function, no post, no duty improved this relationship in cooperation with them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: I see. Do you know if any such personal relations were established at any point between officers of the ABiH and officers of the El Mujahid Detachment?

utterances.speaker: HALIM HUSIC
utterances.text: A number of persons from within the army had more or less influence on them. It was difficult to estimate who had how much influence. There was also a number of representatives of the civilian authorities and also a number of clerics. On the other hand, they attempted an assassination on my colleague, Karalic, who was a theologian, and in respect of certain civilians in the authorities, they referred to them as communists and refused any kind of contact or cooperation with these people. They declared a number of officers as members of the Yugoslav People's Army Intelligence and Security Service, and then there were some people with whom they more or less communicated with a certain degree of trust. But it's difficult to say who had how much influence. Even though I'm a theologian, and I could have been close to them, based on certain attributes, from the first days in Mehurici I had a conflict with them when I began to tell them that there was a large number of individuals among them who were working for foreign services, who were creating problems for us and for them, who were obstructing our fight, and for this reason even my security was in jeopardy for a certain period of time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you very much, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Any re-examination, madam -- I beg your pardon. Questions arising from the questions by the Bench, Madam Vidovic?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very brief ones, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Please, you talked about the humanitarian assistance that you talked about in response to Judge Harhoff's question, the assistance that these Arabs provided, and you talked about the relationship of the civilian authorities with them. My question is this: What was your understanding of this problem of these foreign fighters, the Mujahedin? Based on that understanding, can you please tell Their Honours, was this a military or a political issue in Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: HALIM HUSIC
utterances.text: It was primarily a political issue, because actually without the humanitarian assistance, it was not possible to feed the population, and this is something that is in the domain of the civilian authorities. Then there are these other activities which, to a certain degree, touched upon the military units in certain parts of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. Your Honours, I have no further questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Neuner.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Good morning again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: It's in the afternoon now, Mr. Neuner.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Good afternoon, then. I have a question in relation to what you have said a moment ago when you were asked about Judge Harhoff about personal relations which were established between the army or members in the army and members of the El Mudjahedin Detachment, and you said a number of persons from within the army had more or less influence on them. Could you name those persons, please?

utterances.speaker: HALIM HUSIC
utterances.text: It would be difficult. Among the officers in the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina, there were a number of people who would carry out the practices required by them of Islam, so this was the first thing that they would look at. Secondly, there was a number of persons who -- in some segments who -- well, this is questionable, but they considered them to have religious signs in the conduct or in the way they looked, for example, their beards or how they behaved towards people, but they actually made their own assessments. I know that they did take into account the opinions of the 3rd Corps commander to a certain degree, but, on the other hand, it would happen that they would completely ignore or refuse to follow his orders. So it's hard to say this precisely. They would decide who, when, and to what extent they would cooperate or listen to any particular person.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Could you name the 3rd Corps commander you're referring to?

utterances.speaker: HALIM HUSIC
utterances.text: The commander of the 3rd Corps was Mr. Sakib Mahmuljin.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Who else, other than Sakib Mahmuljin, can you recall?

utterances.speaker: HALIM HUSIC
utterances.text: I can remember all the people who were in the Corps Command, but not that they were able to cooperate with the members of the El Mudjahedin Detachment, just like he couldn't cooperate with them all the time. How do you mean "who else"?

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: For those who had a relationship with them, whom they talked to.

utterances.speaker: HALIM HUSIC
utterances.text: I don't know. I wasn't with them to be able to have that sort of insight.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Then this is page 69 and 70, you were asked about danger which may have occurred when combat operations were going on and certain foreigners were either on their own or in a certain coordination participating. Could you tell me, were there occasions of friendly fire in cases that the Mujahedin or members of the El Mudjahedin Detachment were involved?

utterances.speaker: HALIM HUSIC
utterances.text: I cannot answer that question. I don't know. There were casualties during the war, or combat when there were, or El Mujahedin present or not. We were an untrained army, so it's true that we were killed not only by enemy fire but also from friendly fire. But as time went on, and the more we became like an army, the fewer casualties we did have.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Were you ever informed about an occasion of friendly fire coming from the participation of foreigners in combat on the side of the ARBiH?

utterances.speaker: HALIM HUSIC
utterances.text: Well, it's hard for me to pinpoint such cases, but as to the fact that there were conflicts within the units of the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina in combat or out of combat, it's true, but this is something that the military police dealt with, not the morale department. But we did receive reports about things like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: So, in essence, you don't know?

utterances.speaker: HALIM HUSIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: This is on page 71 of today's transcript. You were talking about orders to the shura of the El Mudjahedin Detachment from centres in Milan. Were you ever --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Was it orders to the shura or orders from the shura?

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: I believe -- I can clarify, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Could you explain again what you meant by orders in relation to the shura? And I think you were referring to centres outside Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: HALIM HUSIC
utterances.text: There was a possibility that regardless of the signing of the Dayton Accords, this unit could refuse to disband and could decide to confront the Bosnia-Herzegovina authorities and the Army of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: So you're referring to the time period in or after December 1995, are you?

utterances.speaker: HALIM HUSIC
utterances.text: Yes. It's a longer period when there were intimations that this detachment had to be or needed to be disbanded and that they had to leave Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: I'm just wondering, were you ever participating in such a meeting of the shura of the El Mudjahedin Detachment?

utterances.speaker: HALIM HUSIC
utterances.text: No. This was their internal body which we know existed and which actually commanded that unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: I understand that this was their internal body, but my question is whether you were ever participating?

utterances.speaker: HALIM HUSIC
utterances.text: Could I?

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: So the answer is "no"?

utterances.speaker: HALIM HUSIC
utterances.text: How could I be a participant in that body? No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: I'm just asking for the basis on which you're saying that this shura has received or may have received orders from abroad.

utterances.speaker: HALIM HUSIC
utterances.text: Based on the fact that the military security services, after numerous complaints about all the activities of the El Mujahid Detachment, began to regularly monitor their activities and to inform the Corps Command and the commander about those activities, including what I was talking about a little bit earlier.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: And did you ever see such an order from anyone?

utterances.speaker: HALIM HUSIC
utterances.text: No. Never, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: We were just talking about the Military Security Service on page 79. Could you clarify on which level this Military Security Service was who obtained that information?

utterances.speaker: HALIM HUSIC
utterances.text: The 3rd Corps Command.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: How could the Military Security Service of the 3rd Corps Command obtain such information?

utterances.speaker: HALIM HUSIC
utterances.text: I cannot explain that to you, because I don't know the manner in which the Military Security Service gets this information. They had their own methods of work. They had listening devices. So I never really had much dealings with these kind of activities or methods, so I really cannot give you an answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: I understand the basis is that you had some conversations with members in the 3rd Corps about activities going on in the El Mudjahedin Detachment. Was that information also coming from the General Staff Security Administration?

utterances.speaker: HALIM HUSIC
utterances.text: What would come from the Security Administration from the General Staff would be addressed to the corps security organs, so I really couldn't see or have any information about their activities. All I knew was that part that the 3rd Corps assistant commander for security talked about at the Corps Command meetings. As for the sources of his information, he never referred to them, and I don't know anything about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: You're referring to the assistant commander for security of the 3rd Corps. Could you name him?

utterances.speaker: HALIM HUSIC
utterances.text: At the time, this was Ekrem Alihodzic. Before that, it was Ramiz Dugalic. During my term of office, it was Mr. Alihodzic. I think there was somebody even before Mr. Dugalic, but I don't know who it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: You were referring to meetings at which the 3rd Corps assistant commander for security briefed. Could you tell me in what time frame these meetings took place?

utterances.speaker: HALIM HUSIC
utterances.text: This was in late 1995. This was an activity that lasted for a while. It was not just a matter of one, two, or three meetings. Towards the end of 1995, the problem that was being resolved mainly by the 3rd Corps was the problem of disbanding the El Mujahid Detachment. The reasons and the way of -- for disbanding and the way to do this in the most painless way was something that the 3rd Corps Command was working on.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: I want to come back to -- I want to leave that topic now and come back to what Judge Harhoff had asked you earlier. It was about attempts to establish communications with the Mujahedin or the El Mudjahedin Detachment. And I'm referring now to 1993, because that's how I understood Judge Harhoff had asked about it. Could we have document PT1543 shown on the screen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Before we have document PT1543, can you tell us what you want us to do with document PT6253?

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: I must apologise. I am at this point in time not aware --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: It has not been admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Is this the testimony in the Hadzihasanovic and Kubura case?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: If Your Honours prefer that this is being admitted --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Your Honours are not leading any witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Yes. We would take the position that the relevant portions have been read into the record, and therefore we would not move to admit it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. Madam Vidovic, you were standing up.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I would just now like to draw the attention to the following: Mr. Neuner, the Prosecutor, is now using the opportunity to continue the cross-examination on those portions that he believes were not covered, and I don't see how, especially how this last question arose from the questions of Judge Harhoff.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'm trying to check the question you are referring to.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I think, if the page is still there, it's page 80, line 24-25.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: On our screens, we are on page 20. But let me tell you, what I do have here is that he says: "I want to leave the topic now and come back to what Judge Harhoff asked you about earlier. It was about attempts to establish communications with the Mujahedin or the El Mujahid Detachment, and I'm referring now to 1993 because that's how I understood Judge Harhoff had asked about it." Could we have document PT1543 shown on the screen. I'm not aware of a question having been put at that stage. So when you say you don't understand how the last question put doesn't relate to -- how it relates to what Judge Harhoff had said, I don't know which question you are referring to. I would understand that PT1543 becomes a completely new document.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I had in mind this part of the question which says that there were attempts to establish communication with the El Mudjahedin Detachment in the course of 1993. I think that this is something that was elaborated, and it's not clear to me how this can arise from the question of Judge Harhoff. However, I withdraw my objection, and we can look at the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Madam Vidovic. Mr. Neuner.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Just to explain, I understood Judge Harhoff to inquire in attempts by the civilian or the military authorities in communicating with the El Mudjahedin Detachment, and this document which we see on the screen is from the 11th of August, 1993. Could we maybe -- it's called: "Information on factors affecting the combat operations and units." Could we maybe go for a second to the signature on the last page to see who authored it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Do you recognise the signature?

utterances.speaker: HALIM HUSIC
utterances.text: Yes. This is my signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: I'm interested in a portion of this document which is, in English, on page 4, and in B/C/S we can stay on this page. It's directly above number 4, the last paragraph above number 4. The entire paragraph or the entire section is referred to as the situation in the area of responsibility of the 306th Mountain Brigade. And it is mentioned here in the last paragraph: "An agreement was reached that the relations among units in our area of responsibility should finally be regulated." Could I ask you, did you participate in this agreement?

utterances.speaker: HALIM HUSIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: But you're reporting about it?

utterances.speaker: HALIM HUSIC
utterances.text: This is a report or information for subordinate units that was drafted on the basis of news items in the media or items from the media, which is what we discussed this morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Can I just ask you, because in the next sentence there's several units mentioned, among others, El Jihad. You referred several times to El Jihad. Is this the unit which was based in Poljanice?

utterances.speaker: HALIM HUSIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Under the command of ...

utterances.speaker: HALIM HUSIC
utterances.text: No one's command.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: But if there is an agreement, who would have authority from that unit to enter into an agreement?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Madam Vidovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Objection, Your Honour. This is inviting the witness to speculate, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Neuner.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: If the witness doesn't know, he should just say so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You're not responding to the objection.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: I did not try to invite the witness to speculate. I was just interested in whether he has knowledge about this part. And if he doesn't have knowledge, he may say so. Otherwise, I can withdraw the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Put the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Could you tell me who, within the El Jihad, had authority to enter into an agreement on or around the 11th of August, 1993?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Madam Vidovic is standing up again.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, another objection, the same objection to this question. It really calls for speculation on the part of the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Well, I had ruled that the question may be put. Maybe this question needs to be put differently, Mr. Neuner, if you do want an answer to it. Who, on behalf of this El Jihad entered this agreement?

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Would you please answer that question?

utterances.speaker: HALIM HUSIC
utterances.text: I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Could you tell me, you got this information from the media, from which media did you get it?

utterances.speaker: HALIM HUSIC
utterances.text: The Travnik Radio. Most frequently, we listened to this station, but also some other Croatian forces, and we prepared this information for the subordinate fighters. And here, this is a good demonstration of how bothered we were by this unregulated relationship, and we wanted to show the fighters that we were going to do something about it and demanded of the political authorities to define definitively the areas through which they could have passage and so on. But this is from the radio, information taken from the radio.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Husic, this paragraph that you are being referred to cannot come from the radio. This is something that took place within the army. You're telling us that it was agreed, there was an agreement reached, that relations among units in your area of responsibility should be finally regulated, so that can't come from the radio. It should come from within the army. And, in fact, I'll tell you which parts of the army: The 7th Muslim Brigade, the 314th Mountain Brigade or Motorised Brigade, rather, the 17th something, something, and El Jihad. Those are the parties to the agreement. This cannot come from the radio. Do you agree with me?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I agree with you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: So let's just not refer to the radio when dealing with this paragraph, because this is action that is being -- this action may be taken based on something heard from the radio, but this paragraph doesn't refer to anything that is heard from the radio. It refers to actions that are being taken within the army.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Would you agree that the nature of such an agreement is sensitive?

utterances.speaker: HALIM HUSIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: And if it would be recorded over the radio, it would mean that the HVO could probably listen to it and would thereby get an advantage?

utterances.speaker: HALIM HUSIC
utterances.text: This is information that was forwarded exclusively to the fighters, members of the 306th Mountain Brigade, and the task of the organs for morale, information, propaganda and religious affairs, which I headed, was not only to work with information that had been checked out first, but it was also something that was needed, that the fighters expected to get, and that impaired the morale, so these were things that would be suggested from our service.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Could I ask that the document please be admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The document is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, the document will become Exhibit 1215.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: I want to show you -- okay, first of all, before it disappears, here is mentioning of -- in this paragraph of a meeting with the commander of the 3rd Corps and of the Bosanska Krajina OG, and the commander of other units.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Do you know anything about this meeting?

utterances.speaker: HALIM HUSIC
utterances.text: This is a meeting, and it states so clearly here. It was a meeting that was about to happen, that was announced. I don't know whether it actually was held and whether all the results that were set forth here, that we wanted to include in this information, whether they actually produced them.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: If I could have Exhibit 257 being shown. Before it comes up, it's a document from the 20th of August, 1993, entitled: "Delivery of information on military conscripts."

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: We see here, the first line of that note from Mr. Adilovic, refers to a meeting on the 9th of August. Were Mr. Adilovic, as a representative of the 7th Muslim Mountain Brigade, attended a meeting in Krpeljici at the 306th Mountain --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Madam Vidovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I really can't see how this question arises from Judge Harhoff's question or any other Judge's questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Neuner.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: I'm prepared to withdraw the question and the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Neuner.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Could I ask -- because at the end of the re-examination by my learned colleague the issue of the statement taking process last week was mentioned, the Prosecution had so far no opportunity to respond to what was said about the statement taking process, could I ask leave by Your Honours to ask a few questions to this witness?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Any response, Madam Vidovic?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Of course, Your Honour. Of course, this does not arise from your questions, but from my questions, and this kind of procedure is not something that is -- that can be foreseen. But he will have an opportunity to answer in detail on this issue, and it's very probably that we will address the Judges panel on this issue in a while, and he will have the opportunity to address it then.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Do I understand you to say you object to the application for the leave?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. --

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: I apologise, Your Honours. Before the Chamber renders a decision, I would simply telegraph that Mrs. Vidovic has discussed this issue with me, and I do anticipate that it will be raised. I would suggest that if we could put a few questions to this witness and perhaps allow Mrs. Vidovic further re-examination following that, we very well could be in a situation, Your Honours, where issues are raised concerning the taking of the statement of this witness. And if we don't -- if we aren't allowed to put some questions to the witness concerning that issue, we will then be in a situation where either we will have to be simply indicating to Your Honours what happened during the course of the taking of this witness's statement, without the benefit of hearing from the witness, himself, on that point. And I don't want to be in a situation where we're then having to bring in an investigator or Mr. Neuner to describe to Your Honours what happened when this witness's statement was taken, when in fact we have the witness sitting here right now, who can testify about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, I see you're on your feet, madam.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let me say this: Your Honour, first of all, I did say something that did not find its way into the transcript, that this was not something that arises from your questions and is not envisaged by the Rules. In any case, I would like Mr. Neuner, as a member of the team that had interviewed this witness, not be the person who will question this witness on the interview taking from this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Let me be clear I understand you, Madam Vidovic. Are you now saying you are no longer -- can I just make sure I understand you, madam. Are you saying you are no longer objecting to the application for leave to ask questions arising from your questions, provided those questions are not asked by Mr. Neuner? Is that what you are saying?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. My objection is general. I wouldn't want any questions to be asked, if you allow me, but I also object to Mr. Neuner asking these questions, because he was one of the persons who was involved as one of the interviewers.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, I could maybe find a way out or offer something.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: It's past time for breaking. Maybe we should deal with this question tomorrow morning. What is tomorrow, our time of sitting? We're sitting in the afternoon tomorrow. Yes, Court will adjourn to tomorrow at quarter past 2.00 in the afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Friday, the 14th day of March, 2008, at 2.15 p.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 1.47 p.m.,
